title: How the Nintendo Entertainment System Changed Gaming Forever
summary: Josh and Chuck look back at the original Nintendo Entertainment System (NES, called the "Any S" / "NES" in the episode), framed as a holiday nostalgia episode. They cover the North American video game crash, Nintendo's Famicom in Japan and its controller design, the failed Advanced Video System at CES, the Robot (R.O.B.) and its Trojan-horse marketing, the New York test market and national rollout, Super Mario Bros., Nintendo's marketing and licensing lockout chip, peripherals like the Zapper, Power Pad and Power Glove, classic games such as Tetris, Metroid, Contra and Zelda, and the myth of blowing on cartridges. A listener mail correction about Nutter Butter and Nutty Buddy closes the episode.

segments.title: Hosts' personal gaming history and holiday nostalgia
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck share their memories of Nintendo, Atari, PlayStation and other consoles, and explain the episode is a holiday nostalgia piece on the original NES, with a possible future episode on the Nintendo 64.

segments.title: North American video game crash
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1983 North American video game crash, blaming poor games and parent backlash, along with the rise of personal computers. Atari's losses are cited, and they note the crash did not happen in Japan.

segments.title: Nintendo's Famicom and controller design
segments.summary: Nintendo began researching home gaming around 1980, and released the Famicom in Japan in 1983 to rival the Epoch Cassette Vision. The Famicom's controller with a D-pad and A and B buttons is described as the basis for modern controllers. Sales were strong in Japan.

segments.title: Advanced Video System and failed CES debut
segments.summary: Nintendo's first North American attempt, the Advanced Video System with keyboard, cassette drive, joystick and wireless zapper, was shown at the January CES and drew no interest. Retailers were burned by the crash and reluctant to stock consoles.

segments.title: R.O.B. the Robot and redesign for the NES
segments.summary: Lance Barr redesigned the system in about an hour for a July CES return. Nintendo used the R.O.B. robot as a Trojan horse to get the console past parents. R.O.B. was slow and worked with only a couple of games such as Gyromite.

segments.title: New York test market and national rollout
segments.summary: Nintendo shipped consoles to about 500 New York stores on consignment, sold roughly half, and then rolled out nationally without further test markets. Surveys found many buyers were motivated by R.O.B. A cheaper Control Deck with Super Mario Bros. sold quickly for the holidays.

segments.title: Super Mario Bros. and Nintendo marketing
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why Super Mario Bros. changed gaming, citing its depth and secrets. They describe Nintendo's marketing, including a call center, Nintendo Power magazine, and the first championships at Universal Studios Hollywood.

segments.title: Licensing lockout chip and quality control
segments.summary: Nintendo controlled third-party licensing with a lockout chip and limits on the number of games per year, and reviewed game designs. The FTC investigated its licensing practices. Bootleggers such as Tengen tried to get around the chip, and a developer used a voltage spike method, illustrated with Bible Adventures.

segments.title: Peripherals: Zapper, Power Pad, Power Glove
segments.summary: The hosts explain how the Zapper light-detection gun worked with Duck Hunt. They discuss the Power Pad fitness mat and the Power Glove, which did not succeed, and the controller's influence on later controllers.
